newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany says chances good of achieving EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: Germany says chances good of achieving EMU goal.

text.p: Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday Germany had a good chance of fulfilling the deficit goal for European monetary union (EMU) this year, and would make extra efforts if it appeared the target could be missed.

Eurosceptic state premiers Gerhard Schroeder of Lower Saxony and Edmund Stoiber of Bavaria, in the same panel discussion, immediately attacked Rexrodt for appearing to waver in his conviction that Germany would fulfil the criteria and threatening additional austerity measures if it does not.
Hans Olaf Henkel, head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), said that while he strongly favoured the euro, the German government should have a bailout plan.

The two state premiers, who said they did not oppose the euro although they were sceptical of it, make strange bedfellows. Both said the common currency was unlikely to help German efforts to reduce unemployment, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's greatest domestic political challenge.
Schroeder is the opposition Social Democrat polls say could defeat Kohl in the elections slated for 1998.

Stoiber is the hardliner from the Christian Social Union who over the weekend apparently hounded his party president, Finance Minister Theo Waigel, into reaffirming his commitment to a strict adherence to the EMU convergence criteria.
Rexrodt insisted he remained commited to the Euro , "We have good chances of filling the deficit criterion," Rexrodt said. "If we do not fulfil it, we must make renewed efforts."
Later Rexrodt repeated that Germany must do all it can to meet the convergence criteria and qualify for EMU, which is slated to start on January 1, 1999. "We cannot wobble," he said.

Rexrodt repeated Bonn's forecast that economic growth should rebound to 2.5 percent this year, boosting tax revenues and improving Germany's chances of narrowing its budget deficit to three percent of economic output, as required by the Maastricht Treaty for EMU members.

Many observers, including the European Union, forecast Germany's deficit will exceed the target, fueling speculation about a possible delay in the start of EMU. A weakening of the entry criteria to allow Germany in even if it does not qualify would open the door for Italy, which is making heroic efforts to meet the goals though it remains further off the mark.

Germany, whose participation in EMU is seen as crucial to the success of the project, is battling a strongly negative public opinion of the project. Italy, whose participation many Germans see as a threat to EMU, has overwhelming public support.
Schroeder said Germany should seek a delay in the start of EMU if it fails to meet the criteria. "If Germany cannot meet the criteria, we should discuss the timetable," he said.

Prospective EMU participants could also adhere to a narrow-band European exchange rate mechanism and introduce a stricter austerity pact to ensure convergence during a transition period if EMU must be delayed, he said.

Rexrodt's allusion to the possibility of new government austerity measures could endanger the tax reform talks between Kohl and SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine scheduled for Tuesday, unless the government explains how such steps would fit into its budget plans, Schroeder said.
Stoiber said Germany had no political leeway for anything other than a strict interpretation of the three percent Maastricht deficit target.

"Currency union is a marriage with no chance of divorce," Stoiber said. While Stoiber said he sees no alternative to the common currency, everything must be done to ensure that the euro is at least as strong as the mark.
"If in a few years people discover that their life insurance policies do not have the external value they once had, the consequences could be disastrous," Stoiber said.
"The question is whether we can be forced to accept a currency union that we don't want," if developments are not exactly to Germany's liking, he said.

Stoiber was critical of those in the government who claim the point of no return has been passed on the euro, a view he said renders meaningless the complex, multi-tiered approvals process due to take place in the spring of 1998.
Henkel said Germany could be painting itself into a corner by insisting on a strict interpretation of the convergence criteria.
"The government would be well advised to have a back-up plan in case things don't work. We will have to give in on one point or another," Henkel said.
